definitions.text: A mathematical pattern is a predictable arrangement of numbers, shapes, or symbols that follows a specific rule or relationship.
A mathematical structure is typically a rule of a numerical, geometric and logical relationship that holds consistency within a specific domain.
A set is described as a well-defined collection of distinct objects, numbers or elements, so that we may be able to decide whether the object belongs to the collection or not.
A set may be described in words.
A set may be described by listing its elements within brackets.

It is sometimes more convenient or useful to employ the method of set-builder notation in specifying sets. This is done by using a symbol or letter for an arbitrary set member and stating the property common to all the members.
N = The set of natural numbers = {1, 2, 3, …}
W = The set of whole numbers = {0, 1, 2, …}
Z = The set of integers = {0, ±1, ±2, …}
O = The set of odd integers = {±1, ±3, ±5, …}
E = The set of even integers = {0, ±2, ±4, …}
P = The set of prime numbers = {2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, …}
Q = The set of all rational numbers = {x | x = p/q where p, q ∈ Z and q ≠ 0}
Q′ = The set of all irrational numbers = {x | x ≠ p/q, where p, q ∈ Z and q ≠ 0}
R = The set of all real numbers = Q ∪ Q′
A set with only one element is called a singleton set.
The set with no elements (zero number of elements) is called an empty set, null set, or Void set.
Two sets A and B are equal if they have exactly the same elements or if every element of set A is an element of set B.
Two sets A and B are equivalent if they have the same number of elements.
If every element of a set A is an element of set B, then A is a subset of B.
If A is a subset of B and B contains at least one element that is not an element of A, then A is said to be a proper subset of B.
If A is a subset of B and A = B, then we say that A is an improper subset of B.
The set that contains all objects or elements under consideration is called the universal set or the universe of discourse.
The power set of a set S denoted by P(S) is the set containing all the possible subsets of S.
The union of two sets A and B, denoted by A∪B, is the set of all elements which belong to A or B.
The intersection of two sets A and B, denoted by A ∩ B, is the set of all elements that belong to both A and B.
If the intersection of two sets is the empty set, the sets are said to be disjoint.
If the intersection of two sets is non-empty but neither is a subset of the other, the sets are called overlapping sets
The difference between the sets A and B denoted by A−B, consists of all the elements that belong to A but do not belong to B.
The complement of a set A, denoted by A' or A^c relative to the universal set U is the set of all elements of U, which do not belong to A.
The cardinality of a set is defined as the total number of elements of a set.

definitions.term: Principle of inclusion and exclusion for two sets
definitions.text:
Let A and B be finite sets, then
n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B)
and A ∪ B and A ∩ B are also finite.

definitions.term: Principle of inclusion and exclusion for three sets
definitions.text:
If A, B and C are finite sets, then
n(A ∪ B ∪ C) = n(A) + n(B) + n(C) − n(A ∩ B) − n(A ∩ C) − n(B ∩ C) + n(A ∩ B ∩ C)
and A ∪ B ∪ C, A ∩ B, A ∩ C, B ∩ C and A ∩ B ∩ C are also finite.

formulas.formula: A ⊆ B iff ∀ x ∈ A ⇒ x ∈ B
formulas.use: Use to show that A is a subset of B.
Use to find the number of subsets of a finite set.

formulas.formula: A ∪ B = {x | x ∈ A ∨ x ∈ B}
formulas.use: Use to list elements in A, in B, or in both.

formulas.formula: A ∩ B = {x | x ∈ A ∧ x ∈ B}
formulas.use: Use to list elements common to both sets.

formulas.formula: A − B = {x | x ∈ A ∧ x ∉ B}
formulas.use: Use to find elements in A but not in B.

formulas.formula: A' = {x | x ∈ U ∧ x ∉ A} = U − A
formulas.use: Use to find the complement of A in the stated universal set U.

formulas.formula: n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B)
formulas.use: Use for the total in either of two finite sets.

formulas.formula: n(A ∪ B ∪ C) = n(A) + n(B) + n(C) − n(A ∩ B) − n(A ∩ C) − n(B ∩ C) + n(A ∩ B ∩ C)
formulas.use: Use for the total in at least one of three finite sets.

formulas.formula: n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B), when A ∩ B = ∅
formulas.use: Use when the two sets are disjoint.
Use to count the elements in A but not in B.

formulas.formula: A ∪ B = B when A ⊆ B; A ∩ B = A when A ⊆ B
formulas.use: Use when one set is contained in the other.

fullMarks: For a set-builder answer, state both the type of elements and every needed condition or bound; do not leave the set unlimited when the question gives an endpoint.
For tabular form, list each distinct element once inside braces. Use ∅ for no elements; do not confuse ∅ with {0}.
For power-set questions, count the elements of the original set first. Treat a set written as an element, such as {b, c}, as one element when counting.
For complements, write or identify the universal set U first, then list only the elements of U that are not in the given set.
For a Venn-diagram answer, draw and label the rectangle U and every circle. Fill the shared regions first, then the exclusive regions, and show elements outside the circles if required.
For verification questions, calculate both sides separately, show the resulting sets, and finish with the equality statement.
For word problems, define the sets and write the known cardinalities before applying inclusion-exclusion. Show the substitution and arithmetic, then finish with a sentence answering the question.
Cardinality answers count elements or people, not set notation; include the appropriate unit or context in the final sentence.
mistakes: Writing {0} for the empty set. Fix: {0} contains one element; use ∅ or {} when there are no elements.
Treating repeated elements as extra elements in a set or in its cardinality. Fix: list each distinct element only once.
Counting {b, c} as two elements in {a, {b, c}}. Fix: the inner set {b, c} is one element of the outer set.
Finding a complement without using the stated universal set. Fix: write U first and subtract the given set from U.
Reversing a set difference, or assuming A − B = B − A. Fix: A − B keeps elements in A that are not in B; order matters.
In inclusion-exclusion for three sets, subtracting pairwise overlaps but forgetting to add the triple overlap back. Fix: use the full formula and check that the final triple term is added.

In a Venn diagram, putting pairwise intersection totals directly into the pair-only regions when they include the triple intersection. Fix: subtract the triple intersection from each pair total before filling pair-only regions.

shortTheory.question: Define a set.
shortTheory.answer: A set is described as a well-defined collection of distinct objects, numbers or elements, so that we may be able to decide whether the object belongs to the collection or not.

shortTheory.question: What is a proper subset?
shortTheory.answer: If A is a subset of B and B contains at least one element that is not an element of A, then A is said to be a proper subset of B.

shortTheory.question: Define the power set of a set S.
shortTheory.answer: The power set of a set S denoted by P(S) is the set containing all the possible subsets of S.

shortTheory.question: Define the union of two sets.
shortTheory.answer: The union of two sets A and B, denoted by A∪B, is the set of all elements which belong to A or B.

shortTheory.question: Define the intersection of two sets.
shortTheory.answer: The intersection of two sets A and B, denoted by A ∩ B, is the set of all elements that belong to both A and B.

shortTheory.question: What are disjoint sets?
shortTheory.answer: If the intersection of two sets is the empty set, the sets are said to be disjoint.

shortTheory.question: State the principle of inclusion and exclusion for two finite sets.

Let A and B be finite sets, then
n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B)
and A ∪ B and A ∩ B are also finite.
